messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David, a 32-year-old North American male and park ranger, has been struggling with debilitating symptoms following a horrific experience of torture. The trauma left deep scars both physically and emotionally, profoundly affecting his daily life. The event that David endured was searingly vivid in some moments but entirely blank in others. He could recall the intense fear and pain as if it were yesterday, yet he struggled to form a coherent narrative around it. When trying to explain what happened, David often lost track of his thoughts, making it almost impossible for him to articulate the details coherently. David had come to believe that his body was permanently damaged by the torture, leaving him with a sense of physical vulnerability that persisted long after the event. This belief was reinforced every time he felt an intense bodily response before he could even process what was happening around him. His heart would race and his muscles would tense at the slightest hint of danger or discomfort, as if his body were always on high alert. David’s fear of going crazy was a constant companion. He was certain that his exaggerated reactions post-trauma indicated a deep-seated mental instability. This belief made it challenging for him to trust others and rely on them for support. Instead, he found solace in rehearsing conversations before any interaction, meticulously planning every word to prevent the risk of saying something out of place. The fear of driving or being a passenger in a vehicle was another significant issue for David. The trauma had left him with an intense aversion to being enclosed and moving at high speeds, leading him to avoid these situations altogether. This avoidance extended to his daily life as a park ranger. He would often walk long distances instead of using a vehicle, which made his work more arduous and time-consuming. David’s tendency to numb his feelings was another maladaptive strategy he had developed. Whenever the memories of the torture began to surface, he would retreat into emotional numbness, detaching from both his surroundings and himself. This numbing allowed him to continue functioning in his daily life but came at a steep cost, as it prevented him from fully engaging with others or experiencing joy. David’s heightened sense of threat was also palpable. He assumed that any delay in routine activities was a sign of impending danger. For instance, if he expected someone to arrive and they were even slightly late, his mind would immediately jump to the worst-case scenario. This pattern extended to checking doors and windows repeatedly, ensuring that everything was secure multiple times before feeling at ease. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has been profound. David’s relationships have suffered as a result of his avoidance and emotional detachment. His work as a park ranger became increasingly challenging due to his reluctance to use vehicles, which affected his ability to perform some essential duties efficiently. It wasn’t until he realized that his life had become so restricted by fear and avoidance that he finally decided to seek help. What frightened him most was the prospect of continuing in this state indefinitely, unable to trust others or enjoy life fully. He hoped that with professional support, he could regain a sense of control over his thoughts and emotions and live more freely without the constant threat looming over him.
